messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: templight
parts:
I ran this template metaprogram profiler

http://meetingcpp.com/tl_files/2013/talks/Debugging%20TMP%20-%20Porkolab.pdf
http://plc.inf.elte.hu/templight/

on test-unit and it generated 45G of .xml output that I don't really know what to do with. One of the smaller .xml files is attached in zipped form.

They have a tool to visualize these files, but it only works one file at a time and doesn't do much. I can parse them in R using the XML package. Here is a histogram of the memory used for the instantiations logged in the attachment.



But we really need some sort of scheme to process all this info. If we can figure out what instantiations are the most common or the most costly, I think Bob mentioned that there was a way to librarify them?

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] templight
parts: I haven't looked at the output yet, but I wanted to reply to some parts of the email.

On Wed, Nov 27, 2013 at 12:31 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
I ran this template metaprogram profiler

http://meetingcpp.com/tl_files/2013/talks/Debugging%20TMP%20-%20Porkolab.pdf
http://plc.inf.elte.hu/templight/

on test-unit and it generated 45G of .xml output that I don't really know what to do with. One of the smaller .xml files is attached in zipped form.

They have a tool to visualize these files, but it only works one file at a time and doesn't do much. I can parse them in R using the XML package. Here is a histogram of the memory used for the instantiations logged in the attachment.

Can you fill me in on the context? What were you hoping this would give us? My best guess is that you're profiling the compilation, but what change can it affect?

Perhaps take a step back and give me an idea of why you're looking into some of these tools? Just so I know what to look for.

But we really need some sort of scheme to process all this info. If we can figure out what instantiations are the most common or the most costly, I think Bob mentioned that there was a way to librarify them?

Ah... so the key term here is "explicit template instantiation." We already know what template types are possible through the generated code. And we can generate them. I've looked at it on and off for a while, but haven't been able to implement it across the build in a stable manner. I've wanted to go back to it, but it's been pretty busy.

Do you want to help exploring that route?


Daniel

On Wednesday, November 27, 2013 2:15:22 PM UTC-5, Daniel Lee wrote:
Whoa. Just looked through the presentation. Looks cool.

I don't know how to use it, though.

That may be the challenge. Attached is a data.frame called ETAS that you can load() in R that was extracted from the XML files such that Kind is "ExplicitTemplateArgumentSubstitution" and the PointOfInstantiation starts with src/. The other Kinds that may be of interest are:

DeducedTemplateArgumentSubstitution
DefaultFunctionArgumentInstantiation
DefaultTemplateArgumentChecking
DefaultTemplateArgumentInstantiation
Memoization
PriorTemplateArgumentSubstitution
TemplateInstantiation
